investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the PHQ-9 and what is it used for?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A 9-item self-report questionnaire mapping the DSM criteria for depression.It screens for depression, grades its severity, and monitors response to treatment, mainly in primary care.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is the PHQ-9 scored?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Each of the 9 items is scored 0-3 (not at all / several days / more than half the days / nearly every day) for symptoms over the last 2 weeks, giving a total of 0-27.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: State the PHQ-9 severity bands.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 0-4 none/minimal
  • 5-9 mild
  • 10-14 moderate
  • 15-19 moderately severe
  • 20-27 severe depression

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why is PHQ-9 item 9 special?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: It asks about thoughts of self-harm or being better off dead.A positive response mandates an immediate suicide risk assessment regardless of the total score.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What PHQ-9 change indicates treatment response?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A reduction of roughly 5 points, or dropping into a lower severity band, is used as a marker of a meaningful response to treatment.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How does the PHQ-9 band steer treatment (NICE NG222)?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Less severe (<16): guided self-help, CBT or behavioural activation (avoid routine antidepressants)
  • More severe (≥16): offer an antidepressant (SSRI first-line, e.g. sertraline) and/or high-intensity psychological therapy, by patient choice
Remission target PHQ-9 <5.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: A patient scores low overall but is positive on item 9 — what do you do?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A positive item 9 (self-harm thoughts) mandates an immediate risk assessment regardless of total: safety plan, means restriction, involve family; urgent same-day crisis-team/CMHT or A&E if high risk.A low total never excludes risk.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the GAD-7 and what does it measure?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A 7-item self-report questionnaire that screens for and measures the severity of generalised anxiety over the last 2 weeks.It is widely used in UK primary care and IAPT and is also sensitive to panic, social anxiety and PTSD.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is the GAD-7 scored?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Each of the 7 items is rated 0 (not at all), 1 (several days), 2 (more than half the days) or 3 (nearly every day) over the last 2 weeks, giving a total of 0-21.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What are the four GAD-7 severity bands?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 0-4 minimal
  • 5-9 mild
  • 10-14 moderate
  • 15-21 severe anxiety
The cut-offs 5/10/15 mark the mild/moderate/severe boundaries.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What GAD-7 score is the usual threshold for likely GAD?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A total of 10 or more (≥10) is the usual threshold suggesting likely GAD and warranting further clinical assessment to confirm the diagnosis.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why must a raised GAD-7 not be treated as a diagnosis?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: It is only a screening/severity tool. A raised score needs clinical assessment to confirm GAD and to exclude organic mimics such as hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, phaeochromocytoma, caffeine/substance use and medication effects.Co-existing depression should be screened with the PHQ-9.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Outline NICE stepped-care drug treatment for GAD.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: SSRI first-line (e.g. sertraline); if ineffective, an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (duloxetine/venlafaxine), then pregabalin; specialist referral for marked impairment/risk.Avoid long-term benzodiazepines (short-term crisis use only).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the GAD-2 and how is it used?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: The first two GAD-7 items (score 0–6) as an ultra-brief anxiety screen; a score ≥3 prompts the full GAD-7.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What does the Y-BOCS measure, and what does it NOT do?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: It measures the severity of OCD independently of symptom content, and tracks treatment response.It is not diagnostic and does not assess risk.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is the Y-BOCS structured and scored?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: 10 items - 5 for obsessions and 5 for compulsions - each scored 0-4, giving a total of 0-40.A symptom checklist accompanies the severity scale.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What five dimensions does each Y-BOCS item rate?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Time occupied
  • interference with functioning
  • distress
  • resistance to symptoms
  • and degree of control over symptoms

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: State the Y-BOCS severity bands.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 0-7 subclinical
  • 8-15 mild
  • 16-23 moderate
  • 24-31 severe
  • 32-40 extreme

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: First-line treatment for OCD?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) and/or an SSRI, often at higher doses and for longer than in depression.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Map Y-BOCS severity to management (NICE).
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Mild (8–15): CBT with ERP
  • Moderate (16–23): SSRI or intensive CBT/ERP
  • Severe/extreme (≥24): combined SSRI + CBT/ERP + specialist OCD referral

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the drug treatment of OCD, including the second-line agent and trial length?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: SSRI first-line, often at higher dose with a longer trial — judge response at ~12 weeks.If ineffective/not tolerated, clomipramine (TCA) is second-line.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is exposure and response prevention (ERP)?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Graded exposure to the feared stimulus while preventing the compulsive response, allowing the anxiety to habituate without performing the ritual — the core psychological treatment for OCD.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What are the two Whooley questions and over what timeframe are they asked?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
Over the past month:
  • (1) Have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?
  • (2) Have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?
They screen for low mood and anhedonia; a 'yes' to either is positive.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is the EPDS structured and scored?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A 10-item self-report questionnaire about the past 7 days; each item scored 0-3, giving a total of 0-30.A cut-off around 10-13 suggests possible depression (approximately 13 for probable major depression).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why is EPDS item 10 particularly important?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Item 10 asks about thoughts of self-harm.Any positive answer mandates an urgent risk assessment regardless of the total score, because the total can be low while suicidal thoughts are present.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How do you distinguish baby blues from postnatal depression?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Baby blues peak around days 3-10 postpartum: tearful, labile, but self-limiting and needing only reassurance.Postnatal depression is persistent low mood/anhedonia emerging over weeks to months and is managed like depression.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What features suggest postpartum psychosis and how is it managed?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Abrupt onset within days to 2 weeks of delivery with confusion, mania, fluctuating mood, delusions/hallucinations, or thoughts of harming self or baby.It is a psychiatric emergency needing same-day specialist assessment and usually admission to a mother-and-baby unit.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is postnatal depression treated, and which antidepressant is preferred in breastfeeding?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Mild → guided self-help/CBT in primary care
  • moderate–severe → specialist perinatal MH referral + an SSRI
Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in a breastfeeding mother (low breast-milk transfer).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Who is at highest risk of puerperal psychosis, and what follows?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
Women with
  • bipolar disorder
  • a previous puerperal psychosis
  • or a family history (recurrence ~1 in 2)
They should have antenatal perinatal mental-health planning; puerperal psychosis itself is a same-day emergency (MBU admission).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What does the SCOFF acronym stand for?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Sick (make yourself sick when too full)
  • Control (lost control over eating)
  • One stone (lost >1 stone / ~6.35 kg in 3 months)
  • Fat (believe self fat when others say thin)
  • Food (does food dominate your life)

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What SCOFF score is a positive screen, and what does it mean?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A score of ≥2 out of 5 'yes' answers is positive and suggests likely anorexia or bulimia nervosa, warranting further assessment.It is a screen, not a diagnosis.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why is a positive SCOFF only the start of assessment?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: SCOFF does not measure severity or medical risk.A positive screen must be followed by BMI, physical examination, and bloods including electrolytes to assess complications and stability.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Which electrolyte disturbance is classically seen with self-induced vomiting or laxative misuse?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
Hypokalaemia is common to both and risks arrhythmia.
  • Vomiting → metabolic alkalosis
  • laxative misuse → metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate lost in stool)
Check U&Es and an ECG.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is refeeding syndrome and which electrolytes fall?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A dangerous shift on re-nourishing a severely malnourished patient, with falling phosphate, potassium and magnesium.It can cause arrhythmias and cardiac failure; re-feed cautiously and use a risk framework (MEED/MARSIPAN).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: A patient screens SCOFF ≥2 — what are the next steps?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Do a full eating-disorder assessment and refer to a specialist/community eating-disorder serviceif medically unstable (very low BMI, bradycardia, electrolyte derangement, long QTc), refer urgently to acute medicine.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What medical-risk investigations follow a positive eating-disorder screen?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• BMI
  • the SUSS test (sit-up/squat-stand for proximal myopathy)
  • ECG (bradycardia, prolonged QTc)
  • bloods U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC ± LFTs
  • risk-stratify with MEED

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the first-line treatment for anorexia and for bulimia nervosa?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Anorexia: psychological therapy first-line (CBT-ED / MANTRA / SSCM; FBT in under-18s)
  • Bulimia: guided self-help / CBT-ED plus fluoxetine

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What do the letters in CAGE stand for, and what score is a positive screen?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Cut down
  • Annoyed
  • Guilty
  • Eye-opener
Each 'yes' scores 1 (0-4). A score of 2 or more suggests problem drinking / probable dependence.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is the AUDIT structured and scored?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
10 items each scored 0-4, total 0-40.
  • Items 1-3 = consumption
  • 4-6 = dependence
  • 7-10 = alcohol-related harm
AUDIT-C uses only the first 3 consumption questions (0-12).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: State the key AUDIT thresholds.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 8+ = hazardous/harmful drinking (give brief intervention)
  • 20+ = possible dependence (refer for specialist assessment)
AUDIT-C positive at ≥5 in men, ≥4 in women.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is alcohol dependence managed versus hazardous use?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Hazardous/harmful use: structured brief advice
  • Dependence: assisted (supervised) withdrawal with benzodiazepines plus relapse-prevention drugs such as acamprosate and psychosocial support, with thiamine throughout

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why must thiamine be given before glucose in a dependent drinker?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.Give parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) first to prevent it.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Which blood tests support a picture of chronic excess alcohol (and what is their limitation)?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Raised GGT
  • raised MCV (macrocytosis)
  • AST:ALT >2:1
  • and raised CDT
They are supportive only — the diagnosis rests on the screening questionnaire plus history, not bloods.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What does medically-assisted alcohol withdrawal involve?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen, dose titrated to withdrawal severity (symptom-triggered, guided by CIWA-Ar), with parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) throughoutthiamine before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke’s.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the AMTS and its cut-off for impairment?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Abbreviated Mental Test Score: a 10-item, ward-based bedside screen scored out of 10.A score of ≤6/10 suggests cognitive impairment and prompts fuller assessment.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the MMSE cut-off and its main weakness?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Mini Mental State Examination is scored /30; roughly <24/30 suggests impairment.It is weak for frontal/executive dysfunction and for mild cases.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why is the MoCA preferred for mild cognitive impairment?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: The MoCA (/30, abnormal <26) includes trail-making, cube/clock drawing and abstraction, making it more sensitive than the MMSE for mild cognitive impairment and for executive/visuospatial deficits.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How does the 6-CIT scoring direction differ from the others?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: The 6-CIT is a short primary-care screen scored inversely: a HIGHER score indicates WORSE cognition, opposite to AMTS/MMSE/MoCA where lower is worse.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What must be excluded before diagnosing dementia from a low screen score?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Delirium (assess attention, e.g. 4AT) and reversible causes: B12/folate, thyroid, calcium, infection, depression (pseudodementia) and medication.Screens are not diagnostic and are confounded by education, language and sensory impairment.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What reversible-cause work-up follows a positive cognitive screen?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Bloods: FBC, U&E, glucose/HbA1c, calcium, LFTs, TFTs, B12/folate (± HIV/syphilis if young-onset/atypical)
  • CT/MRI head to exclude subdural, tumour or NPH
  • then refer to a memory clinic

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Distinguish delirium, dementia and depressive pseudodementia.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating, inattentive (screen 4AT, treat first)
  • Dementia: chronic, progressive
  • Depressive pseudodementia: low mood, poor effort/"don’t know" answers
Always exclude delirium before diagnosing dementia.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Name the 5 statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 1) Presume capacity
  • 2) Support the person to make their own decision
  • 3) An unwise decision does not equal incapacity
  • 4) Acts for those lacking capacity must be in their best interests
  • 5) Choose the least restrictive option

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What are the two stages of the MCA capacity test?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Stage 1 (diagnostic): is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the functioning of the mind or brain?
  • Stage 2 (functional): because of it, is the person unable to Understand, Retain, Use/Weigh, or Communicate the decision?

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What are the four functional abilities a person must be able to do to have capacity?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Understand the relevant information
  • Retain it long enough to decide
  • Use or Weigh it as part of the decision
  • and Communicate the decision by any means

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Why is capacity described as decision-specific and time-specific?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: A person may have capacity for one decision but not another, and capacity can fluctuate over time (e.g. in delirium)so it must be reassessed for each decision at the relevant time and never applied as a global label.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What should you check for once someone is found to lack capacity for a decision?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• A Lasting Power of Attorney (health & welfare)
  • a valid and applicable Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT)
  • and whether an IMCA is needed
then act in the person's best interests using the least restrictive option.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: An incapacitated patient needs urgent treatment and there is no time to assess capacity or find an ADRT/LPA — what do you do?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Treat in best interests under the doctrine of necessity, giving only what cannot safely wait, and reassess when possible.Care does not halt while capacity is documented.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How is a best-interests decision made for someone lacking capacity?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Check for a valid ADRT, then a health-and-welfare LPA or court-appointed deputyotherwise the clinician decides, consulting family/carers (or an IMCA if unbefriended + serious decision), choosing the least-restrictive option and documenting.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Section 2 vs Section 3: purpose and duration?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Section 2 = admission for ASSESSMENT, up to 28 days, not renewable
  • Section 3 = admission for TREATMENT, up to 6 months, renewable
Both need 2 doctors + an AMHP.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is Section 4 and how does it differ from Section 2?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: Section 4 is an EMERGENCY admission lasting 72 hours needing only 1 doctor + AMHP, used when waiting for a second doctor would cause undesirable delay.Section 2 needs 2 doctors and lasts 28 days.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Compare Section 5(2) and Section 5(4).
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• 5(2) = doctor's holding power, 72 hours
  • 5(4) = nurse's holding power, 6 hours
Both apply only to patients ALREADY ADMITTED as inpatients and neither authorises treatment.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Section 136 vs Section 135?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• Section 136 is a police power to remove a person from a PUBLIC place to a place of safety (up to 24 hours)
  • Section 135 is a magistrate's warrant allowing police to enter a PRIVATE property to remove a person

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Do holding powers (5(2)/5(4)) allow treatment, and can they be used in A&E?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: No. Holding powers only prevent the patient leaving until a full assessment;they do not authorise treatment and cannot be used in A&E or the community (patient must be an admitted inpatient).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: Which detained patients get free s117 aftercare, and what is a CTO?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: s117 gives free aftercare after s3 (and s37/47/48) — a joint ICB/local-authority duty that cannot be charged; s2 patients are not entitled.A CTO (s17A) allows supervised community treatment after s3, with power of recall to hospital.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: How do you choose between the MHA and MCA/DoLS?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back:
• MHA: compulsory hospital treatment of a mental disorder in a patient who objects/needs detention
  • MCA/DoLS: a patient who lacks capacity and is not objecting, needing best-interests care (e.g. dementia, physical illness)
The MHA cannot treat a physical illness in a capacitous patient.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.front: What is the Nearest Relative’s role for Sections 2 and 3?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.back: For s3 the AMHP must consult the NR, who can object (blocking admission unless displaced by court) and can order discharge (72h notice; RC may bar).For s2 the NR is informed only and cannot block it.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient completes the PHQ-9 and scores 17. Which severity band does this fall into?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Moderately severe
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A PHQ-9 total of 15-19 corresponds to moderately severe depression. A score of 17 sits squarely within this band, above moderate (10-14) but below severe (20-27).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient scores 3 on the PHQ-9 but endorses item 9, reporting recent thoughts of being better off dead. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure that the low total excludes clinically significant depression
Repeat the PHQ-9 in 6 weeks with no further action now
Start a high-dose antidepressant on the basis of the total score
Discharge back to routine follow-up as the score is minimal
Perform an immediate suicide risk assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Perform an immediate suicide risk assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A positive item 9 mandates an immediate risk assessment irrespective of the total score. A low total does not exclude significant suicide risk, so the number must never be relied upon alone.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: What is the maximum possible total score on the PHQ-9?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The PHQ-9 has 9 items each scored 0-3, giving a maximum of 9 x 3 = 27. The total therefore ranges from 0 to 27 across the severity bands.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient has a PHQ-9 of 22 with no acute risk. According to NICE, what should be offered?
options: An antidepressant (SSRI first-line) and/or high-intensity psychological therapy
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: An antidepressant (SSRI first-line) and/or high-intensity psychological therapy
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A PHQ-9 of 22 is "more severe" depression (≥16). NICE NG222 recommends offering an antidepressant (SSRI first-line) and/or a high-intensity psychological therapy (CBT/IPT), guided by patient choice. Guided self-help alone is for less severe depression.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 19-year-old is started on an SSRI for moderately severe depression. When should they first be reviewed?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Within 1 week
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Patients under 25 (or at increased suicide risk) starting an antidepressant should be reviewed within 1 week because of the early risk of increased agitation/suicidal ideation; others are reviewed at about 2 weeks.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient completes the GAD-7 and scores 16. Which severity band does this represent?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Severe anxiety
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: On the GAD-7 a total of 15-21 falls in the severe anxiety band, so a score of 16 indicates severe anxiety. The cut-offs 5, 10 and 15 mark the mild, moderate and severe boundaries respectively.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: What is the maximum possible total score on the GAD-7?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Each of the 7 items is scored from 0 to 3, giving a maximum total of 7 x 3 = 21. Totals range from 0 to 21 across four severity bands.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 45-year-old woman scores 13 on the GAD-7 alongside palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose GAD on the strength of the GAD-7 score and start an SSRI
Perform clinical assessment and investigate for organic causes such as thyroid dysfunction
Reassure her that a score of 13 excludes any physical illness
Repeat the GAD-7 in 6 months before taking any action
Refer directly for inpatient psychiatric admission
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Perform clinical assessment and investigate for organic causes such as thyroid dysfunction
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The GAD-7 is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, and her somatic features suggest a possible organic mimic such as hyperthyroidism. Clinical assessment and appropriate investigation (e.g. thyroid function) are needed before anxiety is treated as primary.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient has moderate GAD (GAD-7 12) with no organic cause and wants drug treatment. What is the first-line medication?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: An SSRI such as sertraline
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: First-line drug treatment for GAD is an SSRI (e.g. sertraline). SNRIs and pregabalin are later steps; regular benzodiazepines are avoided (dependence) and used only short-term in crises.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: What is the maximum possible total score on the Y-BOCS?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The Y-BOCS has 10 items, each scored 0-4, giving a maximum of 40. Five items rate obsessions and five rate compulsions.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient scores 27 on the Y-BOCS. Which severity band does this represent?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Severe
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A score of 24-31 corresponds to severe OCD. Scores of 32-40 would indicate extreme OCD, and 16-23 moderate.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Which statement about the Y-BOCS is correct?
options: It establishes the diagnosis of OCD
It rates the severity of OCD independently of symptom content
It provides a formal suicide risk assessment
It scores only compulsions, not obsessions
It is a patient-completed depression screen
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: It rates the severity of OCD independently of symptom content
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The Y-BOCS is a clinician-administered severity scale that grades OCD regardless of the specific obsessions or compulsions. It is not diagnostic and does not assess risk, so depression and suicidality must be evaluated separately.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient has a Y-BOCS of 28 (severe OCD). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Combined SSRI and CBT with ERP, plus referral to specialist OCD services
No treatment as Y-BOCS is only a research tool
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Combined SSRI and CBT with ERP, plus referral to specialist OCD services
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Severe/extreme OCD (Y-BOCS ≥24) warrants combined treatment — an SSRI plus CBT with ERP — and referral to specialist OCD services. Self-help alone is for mild disease; benzodiazepines are not a treatment for OCD.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: How long should an SSRI be trialled in OCD before judging response?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: About 12 weeks
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: OCD often needs higher SSRI doses and a longer trial than depression — response is judged at around 12 weeks. Clomipramine is the second-line agent if an SSRI is ineffective or not tolerated.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A woman is 5 days postpartum. Her partner reports she is suddenly confused, elated with pressured speech, expressing bizarre delusional beliefs about the baby, and not sleeping. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure that this is normal baby blues and review in one week
Ask her to complete the EPDS and refer routinely if it is above 13
Arrange same-day specialist perinatal mental-health assessment
Start a low-dose SSRI and review in the community in four weeks
Advise the third Whooley help question and offer self-referral to talking therapy
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Arrange same-day specialist perinatal mental-health assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Abrupt onset within days of delivery with confusion, mania, and delusions is postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. It requires same-day specialist assessment and usually admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Which statement best describes the scoring of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale?
options: 9 items each scored 0-3, total 0-27, diagnostic of depression above 15
2 yes/no questions with a third help question
10 items each scored 0-3, total 0-30, with a cut-off around 10-13
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: 10 items each scored 0-3, total 0-30, with a cut-off around 10-13
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The EPDS has 10 items each scored 0-3, giving a maximum of 30. A cut-off around 10-13 indicates possible depression warranting further assessment.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A postnatal woman scores 8 on the EPDS but answers positively to item 10 about thoughts of self-harm. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The total is below the cut-off, so no further action is needed
The positive self-harm item mandates an urgent risk assessment despite the low total
The result is invalid and the questionnaire should be repeated in two weeks
It confirms a diagnosis of severe postnatal depression
It indicates baby blues and reassurance is sufficient
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: The positive self-harm item mandates an urgent risk assessment despite the low total
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: EPDS item 10 asks about self-harm, and any positive answer overrides the total score. It requires an immediate risk assessment regardless of whether the overall total reaches the depression cut-off.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A breastfeeding mother has moderate postnatal depression needing an antidepressant. Which SSRI is preferred?
options: Any antidepressant must be avoided while breastfeeding
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Sertraline
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because of its low breast-milk levels. Antidepressants are not contraindicated in breastfeeding, and the treatment decision should weigh the benefits of treating depression against minimal infant exposure.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 19-year-old woman answers 'yes' to 3 of the 5 SCOFF questions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The screen is negative as she scored below 4
The screen is positive and warrants further clinical assessment
No action is needed unless her BMI is under 15
She should be discharged with reassurance
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: The screen is positive and warrants further clinical assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A SCOFF score of ≥2 is a positive screen suggesting a likely eating disorder. SCOFF is a screening tool rather than a diagnostic test, so the next step is full assessment of BMI, physical health and risk.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient with bulimia nervosa who vomits several times daily is most likely to show which electrolyte abnormality?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Hypokalaemia
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Recurrent self-induced vomiting causes loss of potassium and hydrogen ions, producing hypokalaemia with a metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalaemia carries a risk of cardiac arrhythmia, so U&Es and an ECG are important.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: When re-nourishing a severely malnourished patient with anorexia nervosa, which biochemical change is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Falling phosphate, potassium and magnesium
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Reintroducing carbohydrate drives insulin release and cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, causing their plasma levels to fall. This can precipitate arrhythmias and cardiac failure, so feeding is introduced cautiously with a risk framework such as MEED/MARSIPAN.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 19-year-old scores 3/5 on SCOFF. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure — a single positive screen means nothing
Start an SSRI and review in 3 months
Full eating-disorder assessment and referral to a specialist eating-disorder service
No action unless BMI is under 15
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Full eating-disorder assessment and referral to a specialist eating-disorder service
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: SCOFF ≥2 is a positive screen warranting a full eating-disorder assessment and referral to specialist services. It is a screen, not a diagnosis; medically unstable patients need urgent acute-medical referral.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Which bedside test best assesses medical risk (proximal muscle weakness) in a patient with anorexia nervosa?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: The sit-up–squat–stand (SUSS) test
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The sit-up–squat–stand (SUSS) test scores the ability to rise from lying and from squatting without using the arms; needing the hands or being unable to rise indicates proximal myopathy and high medical risk (part of MEED risk assessment).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 52-year-old man answers 'yes' to feeling he should cut down and to needing a morning drink to steady his nerves. What does his CAGE result indicate?
options: A positive screen (score ≥2) suggesting problem drinking
Definitive diagnosis of alcohol-related liver disease
Immediate need for inpatient detoxification regardless of other factors
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: A positive screen (score ≥2) suggesting problem drinking
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Two affirmative CAGE answers reach the threshold of ≥2, which screens positive for probable alcohol dependence. This signals the need for further assessment rather than confirming a diagnosis on its own.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient scores 24 on the full AUDIT. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure that this is low-risk drinking
Give a single session of brief advice only
Repeat the AUDIT in five years
Start no intervention until liver enzymes are checked
Refer for specialist assessment as this suggests possible dependence
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Refer for specialist assessment as this suggests possible dependence
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: An AUDIT score of 20 or more suggests possible alcohol dependence and warrants specialist referral. Brief advice alone is insufficient at this level of risk.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A dependent drinker is admitted and stops alcohol abruptly. Which management step is essential to prevent a life-threatening complication?
options: Give oral glucose immediately to prevent hypoglycaemia
Prescribe a benzodiazepine and give parenteral thiamine before any glucose
Withhold all sedatives to monitor consciousness
Restrict fluids to avoid autonomic instability
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Prescribe a benzodiazepine and give parenteral thiamine before any glucose
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Benzodiazepines control withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, while parenteral thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy. Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a deficient patient.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient scores AUDIT 12 (hazardous/harmful drinking) but is not dependent. What is the most appropriate next step?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: A structured brief (motivational) intervention
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: An AUDIT of 8–19 indicates hazardous/harmful drinking, best managed with a structured brief/motivational intervention in primary care. Specialist referral and assisted withdrawal are reserved for likely dependence (higher scores).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: An 82-year-old inpatient scores 5/10 on the AMTS. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The result confirms a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
The score is normal for age and needs no action
The score suggests cognitive impairment and warrants further assessment
The result proves the patient has capacity for all decisions
The score reliably distinguishes delirium from dementia
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: The score suggests cognitive impairment and warrants further assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: An AMTS of ≤6/10 flags likely cognitive impairment and triggers formal assessment, collateral history, bloods and imaging. It is a screening tool, so it neither confirms a specific diagnosis nor distinguishes delirium from dementia.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Which cognitive screen is most sensitive for detecting mild cognitive impairment and executive/visuospatial deficits?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: MoCA
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The MoCA includes trail-making, cube and clock drawing and abstraction tasks, giving it greater sensitivity for mild cognitive impairment and executive/visuospatial domains. The MMSE is comparatively weak in these areas and for mild cases.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient with acute confusion after a hip fracture scores poorly on the MMSE. What should be done before diagnosing dementia?
options: Exclude and treat delirium and reversible causes first
Record dementia as the confirmed diagnosis
Repeat the MMSE hourly until it improves
Refer directly for end-of-life care planning
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Exclude and treat delirium and reversible causes first
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A screen cannot separate delirium from dementia, so acute delirium must be assessed (e.g. attention/4AT) and treated first. Reversible causes such as B12/folate, thyroid, calcium, infection, depression and medication must also be excluded before diagnosing dementia.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: An 80-year-old scores below threshold on a cognitive screen with no acute confusion. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose Alzheimer’s disease and start a cholinesterase inhibitor
Repeat the same screen in 2 years
Reversible-cause bloods and CT/MRI head, then refer to a memory clinic
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Reversible-cause bloods and CT/MRI head, then refer to a memory clinic
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A positive screen is not a diagnosis. Exclude reversible causes (bloods: TFTs, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, U&E, LFTs) and structural mimics (CT/MRI head — subdural, tumour, NPH), then refer to a memory clinic for formal assessment. First exclude delirium if onset is acute/fluctuating.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A 78-year-old man with early dementia insists on going home despite clear risks. He understands and retains the information, weighs it, and clearly communicates his choice. Under the MCA 2005, how should this be interpreted?
options: He lacks capacity because he has a diagnosis of dementia
He can be detained in his best interests without further assessment
He has capacity for this decision; an unwise choice does not equal incapacity
He automatically lacks capacity for all decisions
Capacity cannot be assessed while dementia is present
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: He has capacity for this decision; an unwise choice does not equal incapacity
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: He satisfies all four functional abilities, so Stage 2 is not met and he retains capacity for this decision. A diagnosis alone never removes capacity, and the third statutory principle confirms an unwise decision does not indicate incapacity.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Which sequence correctly describes the two-stage MCA capacity test?
options: First assess best interests, then check for an impairment of mind or brain
First test Gillick competence, then apply the four functional abilities
First obtain an IMCA, then assess understanding only
First check for a Lasting Power of Attorney, then presume incapacity
First confirm an impairment of mind/brain, then whether the person can Understand, Retain, Use/Weigh or Communicate
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: First confirm an impairment of mind/brain, then whether the person can Understand, Retain, Use/Weigh or Communicate
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Stage 1 is the diagnostic test for an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Stage 2 is the functional test asking whether, because of that impairment, the person is unable to understand, retain, use/weigh, or communicate the decision.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient with capacity previously completed a valid and applicable Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment declining blood transfusion. She now lacks capacity and needs transfusion to survive. What is the correct action under the MCA 2005?
options: Transfuse because saving life overrides the advance decision
Respect the ADRT and withhold the transfusion
Ask an IMCA to overrule the advance decision
Transfuse because she now lacks capacity
Seek a best-interests decision that ignores her prior wishes
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Respect the ADRT and withhold the transfusion
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A valid and applicable ADRT is legally binding and must be respected even when the refusal risks death. It represents the capacitous wishes of the person and takes precedence over a best-interests transfusion.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: An unconscious patient in resus needs an immediate life-saving procedure; no ADRT, LPA or family is available. What is the correct action?
options: Wait until a formal capacity assessment is documented
Withhold treatment until a next of kin consents
Apply for a court order first
Provide the necessary treatment in best interests under the doctrine of necessity
Refer to psychiatry for a capacity opinion
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Provide the necessary treatment in best interests under the doctrine of necessity
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity and treatment cannot safely wait, the doctrine of necessity permits acting in their best interests, giving only what is immediately required. A valid, applicable ADRT would override this, but none is available here.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A voluntary inpatient on a medical ward with new-onset psychosis tries to leave; no doctor is immediately available and staff fear for his safety. Which power can the ward nurse use to detain him?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Section 5(4)
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Section 5(4) is the nurse's holding power, lasting up to 6 hours, used for an admitted inpatient when no doctor is immediately available. It buys time for a doctor to review and, if needed, convert to a Section 5(2).

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient with a well-established diagnosis of schizophrenia relapses and needs compulsory hospital admission for ongoing treatment. Which section is most appropriate?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Section 3
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Section 3 is admission for treatment, lasting up to 6 months and renewable, and is used when the mental disorder is already known. It requires two doctors and an AMHP.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: Police find a distressed man behaving erratically on a busy high street and believe he has a mental disorder. Which power lets them take him to a place of safety for assessment?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Section 136
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Section 136 empowers police to remove a person who appears mentally disordered from a public place to a place of safety, for up to 24 hours, to arrange an MHA assessment. Section 135 would be needed for entry to a private dwelling.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A young man with no psychiatric history presents with a first episode of possible psychosis; he refuses admission but needs inpatient assessment to clarify the diagnosis. Which section is most appropriate?
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: Section 2
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: A first presentation needing admission for assessment of an unclear diagnosis is Section 2 (up to 28 days, 2 doctors + AMHP). Section 3 is for treatment of a known disorder; s5(2) is only for existing inpatients.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A patient is discharged after treatment under Section 3. Which is correct regarding aftercare?
options: They are entitled to free s117 aftercare
They must pay for any aftercare
Aftercare requires a new Mental Health Act assessment
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: They are entitled to free s117 aftercare
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: Section 117 imposes a joint ICB/local-authority duty to provide free aftercare to patients discharged from s3 (and s37/47/48); it cannot be charged for. Patients detained only under s2 are not entitled to s117 aftercare.

investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.question: A capacitous adult who has taken an overdose but has no mental disorder refuses medical treatment. Can the Mental Health Act be used to treat him against his wishes?
options: Yes — use Section 2 to enforce medical treatment
Yes — use Section 5(2) on the medical ward
No — the MHA cannot override a capacitous refusal of treatment for a physical illness
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.answer: No — the MHA cannot override a capacitous refusal of treatment for a physical illness
investigations__PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__.explanation: The MHA authorises treatment of mental disorder, not unrelated physical illness. A capacitous patient’s refusal of medical treatment stands; the correct step is to assess capacity, not to section him for a physical problem.
